questions.question: What workload is HDFS primarily designed for?
options: Large files read and written sequentially for batch or analytical processing
Millions of tiny records updated randomly with single-digit millisecond latency
Shared POSIX files edited concurrently by many users
Serving transactional database indexes
questions.explanation: HDFS uses large blocks and streaming I/O to maximize aggregate throughput. It is not a low-latency random-update filesystem.

questions.question: A cluster has 60 nodes with 40 TB each and replication factor three. Before operating reserve, how much logical capacity is available?
options: 800 TB
200 TB
questions.explanation: Raw capacity is 60 x 40 = 2,400 TB. Three physical copies reduce logical capacity to 800 TB before reserve and other overhead.

questions.question: Why are millions of files smaller than one HDFS block a design risk?
options: Each file and block consumes NameNode namespace metadata even when little disk capacity is used
Small files automatically receive no replicas
DataNodes cannot store files below 128 MB
Kerberos cannot authenticate small-file reads
questions.explanation: HDFS can store small files, but the NameNode tracks file and block metadata. Tiny files create namespace and scheduling pressure disproportionate to their bytes.

questions.question: What role does the NameNode play during a normal file read?
options: It returns block locations, after which the client reads data directly from DataNodes
It streams every file byte through its own memory
It decompresses every block for the client
It stores the only copy of every data block
questions.explanation: The NameNode coordinates namespace and block locations. Data transfer happens directly between clients and DataNodes so the metadata service is not the data-path bottleneck.

questions.question: The active NameNode disappears, but all DataNodes remain healthy. What is the first correct recovery action in a high-availability cluster?
options: Fence the old active and promote the synchronized standby
Run the DataNode balancer
Increase the replication factor
Promote the SecondaryNameNode as a hot standby
questions.explanation: Failover must prevent split brain and preserve namespace consistency. The SecondaryNameNode creates checkpoints; it is not the HA standby.

questions.question: Why should a cluster retain material free capacity instead of filling every DataNode?
options: Re-replication, balancing, ingest bursts, and node failures need disk and bandwidth headroom
HDFS deletes replicas when disks exceed 50% utilization
Unused disks improve checksum algorithms
The NameNode cannot track full disks
questions.explanation: A full cluster cannot restore lost replicas or rebalance safely. Operating reserve is part of the recovery design, not wasted capacity.

questions.question: A reader detects a checksum mismatch on one replica. What should the system do?
options: Stop serving the corrupt copy, read a verified replica, and reconstruct healthy replication
Return the corrupt bytes because another replica probably matches
Restart the NameNode and keep the replica
Reduce the file's replication factor
questions.explanation: Checksums make corruption observable. HDFS should use a good replica, quarantine the bad copy, and restore the target replica count.

questions.question: When is erasure coding usually preferable to triple replication?
options: Large, colder datasets where storage efficiency matters and repair/compute cost is acceptable
Every small hot file with frequent appends
NameNode metadata journals
Data that must survive with only one fragment
questions.explanation: Erasure coding reduces storage overhead for suitable large datasets, but reconstruction and write paths are more complex than straightforward replication.
